passages.source_text: Ἐκβάντες οὖν τὴν Τρίπολιν τῆς Φοινίκης ὡς ἐπὶ Ἀντιόχειαν τῆς Συρίας ἐλθεῖν, αὐτῆς ἡμέρας ἐν Ὀρθωσίᾳ ἐμείναμεν ἐλθόντες. καὶ διὰ τὸ πλησίον εἶναι ἧς ἐξήλθομεν πόλεως, πάντων σχεδὸν προακηκοότων τοῦ κηρύγματος, μιᾶς ἡμέρας ἐκεῖ μείναντες ἀπήραμεν εἰς Ἀντάραδον. πολλῶν δὲ τῶν συνοδοιπορούντων ἡμῖν ὄντων, ὁ Πέτρος Νικήτῃ καὶ Ἀκύλᾳ προσομιλεῖ λέγων Ἐπειδὴ πολὺς ὄχλος τῶν συνοδοιπορούντων οὐ μικρὸν φθόνον ἡμῖν εἰσιοῦσιν κατὰ πόλιν ἐπισπᾶται, ἀναγκαίως ἐσκεψάμην φροντίσαι πῶς μήτε οὗτοι λυπηθῶσιν κωλυθέντες συνεῖναι ἡμῖν μήτε ἡμεῖς περίβλεπτοι γινόμενοι φθόνῳ τῷ τῆς κακίας ὑποπέσωμεν. τούτου ἕνεκεν βούλομαί σε τὸν Νικήτην καὶ Ἀκύλαν προοδεύειν μου κατὰ συστήματα δύο σποράδην μονωθέντας τε τὰς τῶν ἐθνῶν εἰσέρχεσθαι πόλεις.

οἶδα δὲ ὅτι ἀθυμεῖτε τοῦτο ποιεῖν ἀκηκοότες, ἀπολειπόμενοί μου διάστημα οὐδ’ ὅλων ἡμερῶν δύο. εἰδέναι οὖν ὑμᾶς θέλω ὅτι πολλαπλάσιον ἀγαπῶμεν ἡμεῖς οἱ πείσαντες ὑμᾶς τοὺς πεισθέντας ἤπερ ὑμεῖς ἡμᾶς τοὺς πεπεικότας. ἀλλήλους οὖν στέργοντες, τῷ μὴ ἀλόγως ποιεῖν ἃ θέλομεν τῆς ἀσφαλείας ὅσον τὸ ἐφ’ ἡμῖν φροντίζωμεν. πρὸς τούτοις δὲ οὐδεμιᾶς ἡμέρας διαλεγομένου μου ἀπελιμπάνεσθε. εἰς γὰρ τὰς ἐπισημοτέρας τῶν ἐπαρχιῶν πόλεις προῄρημαι (ὡς ἴστε καὶ ὑμεῖς) ἡμερῶν ἐπιμένειν καὶ διαλέγεσθαι. καὶ τὸ νῦν εἰς τὴν ἐγγυτέραν ἡμῖν Λαοδίκειαν προάξατε καὶ μεθ’ ἡμέρας δύο ἢ τρεῖς (ὅσον ἐπὶ τῇ ἐμῇ προαιρέσει) καταλήψομαι ὑμᾶς. ἐπὶ δὲ τῶν πυλῶν ἐκδέξασθέ με, ὑμεῖς μόνοι διὰ τὸν θρῦλον, ἵνα οὕτως ἀψοφητὶ συνεισελθόντες ἅμα ὑμῖν ὦμεν. κἀκεῖθεν ὁμοίως μετὰ τὸ ἐπιμεῖναι ἡμερῶν ἄλλοι ἀνθ’ ὑμῶν εἰς τὰ ἐπέκεινα κατὰ ἐφημερίας προάξωσιν, τὰς ξενίας ἑτοιμάζοντες.

ταῦτα τοῦ Πέτρου εἰπόντος ἠναγκάσθησαν συνθέσθαι λέγοντες Οὐ πάνυ ἡμᾶς, κύριε, λυπεῖ τοῦτο πράττειν διὰ τὸ ὑπὸ σοῦ κελεύεσθαι. πρῶτον μέν, ὅτι πάντα καλῶς νοεῖν τε καὶ συμβουλεύειν, ἄξιος ὤν, ὑπὸ τῆς τοῦ θεοῦ προνοίας ἐξελέγης· πρὸς τούτοις δέ, ἐπεὶ ἐπὶ τὸ πολὺ ἡμερῶν δύο ἀνάγκῃ τοῦ προάγειν ἀπολιμπανόμεθά σου. καὶ αὗται μὲν πολλαὶ πρὸς τὸ μὴ σὲ τὸν κύριον ἡμῶν ὁρᾶν Πέτρον, πλὴν λογιζόμεθα ὅτι πλεῖον λυπηθήσονται οἱ πολὺ μακρὰν προπεμπόμενοι ὡς ἐπὶ πλεῖον ἀναμένειν σε κατὰ πόλιν κεκελευσμένοι, ἀνιώμενοι ἐν τῷ ἐπὶ πλεῖον ἐστερῆσθαι τοῦ ὁρᾶν σου τὸ περιπόθητον πρόσωπον. καὶ ἡμεῖς οὐχ ἐλάττονα ἐκείνων ἀθυμοῦντες ὡς κελεύεις διὰ τὸ συμφέρον ποιεῖν οὐκ ἀντιλέγομεν. ὁμῶς ταῦτα εἰπόντες προῆξαν, ἐντολὴν ἔχοντες ἐν τῷ πρώτῳ πανδοχείῳ προσομιλῆσαι τῷ συνοδοιποροῦντι ὄχλῳ, ὅπως σποράδην ἀλλήλων γενόμενοι εἰς τὰς πόλεις εἰσέρχωνται.

πορευθέντων· οὖν αὐτῶν ἐγὼ Κλήμης μεγάλως ἔχαιρον ὅτι σὺν αὐτῷ με ἐκέλευσεν εἶναι. καὶ ἀποκριθεὶς εἶπον Εὐχαριστῶ τῷ θεῷ ὅτι με οὐκ ἐξαπέσταλκας ὡς τοὺς ἑταίρους, ἐπειδὴ ὀδυνώμενος ἂν διαπεφωνήκειν. ὁ δὲ ἔφη Τί δέ; εἰ καὶ χρεία τις ἔσται πεμφθῆναι σέ που μαθημάτων χάριν, σὺ διὰ τὸ πρὸς ὀλίγον ἀπολιμπάνεσθαί μου συμφερόντως, διὰ τοῦτο τεθνήξει; οὐχὶ δὲ προσομιλήσας σεαυτῷ φέρειν τὰ διὰ τὴν ἀνάγκην σοι προσταγέντα εὐθύμως ὑποσταίης; ἢ οὐκ οἶσθα ὅτι σύνεισιν αἰεὶ οἱ φίλοι ταῖς μνήμαις, κἂν τοῖς σώμασιν ἀπολιμπάνωνται; ὡς ἔνιοι συνόντες τοῖς σώμασιν ἀμνημοσύνης αἰτίᾳ τὰς ψυχὰς ἀποδημοῦσιν τοῖς φίλοις.

κἀγὼ ἀπεκρινάμην Μὴ τοίνυν νομίσῃς, κύριε, ὅτι τὰ λύπης πάσχειν ἤμελλον ἀνοήτως, ἀλλὰ καὶ πάνυ ὀρθῷ τινὶ λογισμῷ. ἐπεὶ γὰρ σέ, κύριέ μου, ἀντὶ πάντων ἔχω, πατρός τε καὶ μητρὸς καὶ ἀδελφῶν καὶ συγγενῶν, αἴτιόν μοι γενόμενον διὰ τὸν θεὸν τῆς σωζούσης ἀληθείας, ἀντὶ πάντων ἔχων σε παραμυθίας τῆς μεγίστης τυγχάνω. πρὸς τούτοις δεδιὼς μου καὶ τῆς ἀκμῆς τὴν ἐκ φύσεως ἐπιθυμίαν, ἠγωνίων μήπως ἀπολειφθείς σου, ἄνθρωπος ὢν νεώτερος, ὅπερ νῦν οὕτως ἐνστάσεως ἔχω, κἂν κατὰ τινὰ χόλον θεοῦ ἀποστῆναί σου ἀδύνατον εἰ ἥττων ἐπιθυμίας ἔσομαι. ἀλλ’ ἐπειδὴ πολλῷ ἄμεινον καὶ ἀσφαλέστερον συνεῖναί με σοί, τούτῳ ᾧ ὁ νοῦς μου αἰδεῖσθαι εὐλόγως προείληφεν, διὸ πάντοτέ σοι συνεῖναι εὔχομαι. πρὸς τούτοις δὲ μέμνημαί σου ἐν Καισαρείᾳ εἰπόντος Εἴ τις βούλεταί μοι συνοδεῦσαι, εὐσεβῶς συνοδευέτω. εὐσεβῶς δὲ ἔφης τὸ μηδένα λυπεῖν κατὰ θεόν, οἷον ἀπολιπόντα γονεῖς, γυναῖκα ὁμόφρονα ἢ ἑταίρους τινὰς τῇ θεοσεβείᾳ προσκειμένους. ὅθεν ἐγὼ κατὰ πάντα ἐπιτήδειος εἰμί σοι συνοδοιπόρος, ᾧ εἰ καὶ τὰ μέγιστα χαρίζῃ, τὰς δούλων μοι ὑπηρεσίας συγχωρεῖς ποιεῖν.

context.translation_policy_text:
# Translation Stance

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Contested terms

The following terms appear frequently and carry heavy theological
weight. Our default rendering and rationale are recorded here.
Per-verse variance is documented in the individual YAML files.

| Greek / Hebrew | Default English | Alternatives considered | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Χριστός *Christos* | Messiah where independently titular; Christ in the name forms "Jesus Christ" / "Christ Jesus" | Christ, Messiah | Preserves the title's Hebraic messianic meaning while using the recognizable conventional English personal name |
| κύριος *Kyrios* | Lord | LORD, Master | Matches covenantal and NT usage |
| δοῦλος *doulos* | servant | bondservant, slave | Uses reader-facing "servant" consistently; documents bonded-status and ownership nuance in notes/audit metadata |
| πίστις *pistis* | faith | faithfulness, trust | Main text: faith; footnote alternatives where contested |
| δικαιοσύνη *dikaiosynē* | righteousness | justice | Both renderings preserved in footnotes for Pauline passages |
| ἱλαστήριον *hilastērion* | atoning sacrifice | propitiation, mercy seat | Dynamic rendering for accessibility; alternatives footnoted |
| ἀγάπη *agapē* | love | charity (archaic) | Lexical cognates in source kept |
| σάρξ *sarx* | flesh (literal) / sinful nature (metaphorical) | — | Context-dependent; per-verse documented |
| μετανοέω / μετάνοια *metanoeō / metanoia* | reorient / reorientation; toward God where the context warrants making the destination explicit | repent / repentance (traditional); reconsider / change of mind in documented exceptions | See "Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)" below; do not homogenize regret, divine relenting, or distinct turning words |
| νήφω *nēphō* | clear-minded (most contexts); sober (where Paul explicitly runs the drunk/sober metaphor) | sober-minded | See revision notes in 1 Pet 5:8, 1 Thess 5:6 |
| יְהוָה YHWH | Yahweh | the LORD, Jehovah | Renders the divine name as a name. Where the NT quotes an OT YHWH passage using *Kyrios*, the NT verse retains "Lord" to preserve the Greek; the OT source verse uses "Yahweh". |
| אָדָם *adam* | man / humankind (context) | — | Context-dependent per usage |

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.

## Change log for this document

Material changes to this document are themselves commits. Prior
versions of the stance are preserved in git history.

- **2026-04-21:** Removed creedal affirmations (Apostles' Creed,
  Nicene Creed, Chalcedonian Definition) and replaced with a
  theological-stance section that declines specific creedal
  commitment. Translation philosophy and contested-terms table
  preserved unchanged; those are methodology, not creedal
  commitment, and the project actually runs on them. Added a
  "Translating into other languages" section stating POB's long-
  term intention to ship in every feasible major language, with
  the full revision pipeline and transparent supported-language
  disclosure. Per-verse YAML citing the old `doctrine_reference`
  values is preserved as historical record; those are not
  retroactively edited.
context.ambiguity_review_standard: Apply the supplied DOCTRINE.md ambiguity policy: a defensible contextual rendering may be used in the main text when material alternatives and the reason for the choice are preserved in notes. A unique or uncontested interpretation is not required. Distinguish (a) an unreadable or unverified source, omitted content, invented restoration, or a construction for which no defensible English can be given, from (b) ordinary lexical, attachment, or referent ambiguity faithfully preserved in English or explained with viable alternatives. The former blocks publication; the latter does not automatically block it. A note cannot excuse unsupported wording: the proposed main rendering must itself be defensible from the supplied Greek. Clearly printed gaps must remain gaps, not be filled by invention. Never change a verdict merely to achieve acceptance.
context.selected_edition_coverage_standard: Coverage is assessed against ALL SURVIVING WORDING AND PRINTED GAP MARKERS in the selected image-checked edition, not against unavailable words of a hypothetical complete original. A confirmed printed lacuna must remain an explicit gap in the English, retaining the exact number of printed dots (layout whitespace may differ), with a source-quoted note explaining that its content is unavailable and no restoration has been supplied. Such faithful representation can pass selected-edition coverage; it must never be described as recovery of the lost wording or an unbroken original. Distinguish this from missing scan pages, unverified ink, omitted surviving Greek, an unsupported English completion, or a translation that obscures the gap: those remain blocking. Neither this scope clarification nor a prior suggestion is an instruction to accept a draft; independently check every surviving clause, every gap, and every disclosure.

passages.text: After leaving Tripolis in Phoenicia to make our way toward Antioch in Syria, we came to Orthosia and stayed there that same day. Because it was near the city we had left, and almost everyone there had already heard the proclamation, we stayed there one day and departed for Antaradus. Since many people were traveling with us, Peter spoke to Nicetas and Aquila, saying, “Because the large crowd of those traveling with us attracts no small amount of envy toward us as we enter each city, I have thought it necessary to consider how to ensure that neither these people are distressed by being prevented from staying with us nor we, by becoming conspicuous, fall prey to the envy born of malice. For this reason, I want you, Nicetas, and Aquila to go ahead of me separately, as two parties, each on his own, and to enter the Gentile cities.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Ἐκβάντες οὖν τὴν Τρίπολιν τῆς Φοινίκης ὡς ἐπὶ Ἀντιόχειαν τῆς Συρίας ἐλθεῖν
lexical_decisions.chosen: After leaving Tripolis in Phoenicia to make our way toward Antioch in Syria
lexical_decisions.rationale: The construction presents Antioch as the intended direction or destination of the journey, not as a place already reached.
The prefix προ- indicates prior hearing; κήρυγμα denotes the message proclaimed or the act of proclamation.
The genitive links the envy with κακία, which may denote malice or wickedness; the rendering avoids treating all envy as a separately personified power.

lexical_decisions.chosen: separately, as two parties, each on his own
lexical_decisions.rationale: The wording depicts Nicetas and Aquila as divided into two units and isolated from the larger company. Alternatively, κατὰ συστήματα δύο could be understood as “in groups of two,” but the participle agrees with the two named men.
Here τὰ ἔθνη designates the non-Jewish peoples; “cities of the nations” is a more literal alternative.

passages.text: “I know that, now that you have heard this, you are disheartened about doing it, although you will be separated from me for an interval of not even two full days. I therefore want you to know that we who persuaded you love you who were persuaded many times more than you love us who persuaded you. Since we love one another, then, let us take thought for safety, as far as lies with us, by not irrationally doing whatever we want. Besides, you will not be away from me on any day when I am giving a discourse. For I have decided—as you yourselves know—to stay for days and discourse in the more prominent cities of the provinces. For now, go ahead to Laodicea, which is nearer to us, and after two or three days—as far as it depends on my own choice—I will catch up with you. Wait for me at the gates, you alone, because of the commotion, so that by entering together without noise we may be with you. From there, likewise, after we have stayed for days, others in your place should go ahead in daily rotation to the places beyond, preparing the lodgings.”

lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb expresses loss of heart or discouragement rather than simple sadness.
πολλαπλάσιον gives a comparative idea of manifold or many-times-greater love.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῷ μὴ ἀλόγως ποιεῖν ἃ θέλομεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: by not irrationally doing whatever we want
lexical_decisions.rationale: The articular infinitive is instrumental, explaining how they are to attend to their safety.

lexical_decisions.chosen: you will not be away from me on any day when I am giving a discourse
lexical_decisions.rationale: The promise is that their brief advance journey will not cause them to miss any day on which Peter teaches.
θρῦλος can denote noise, public stir, or widespread talk; the concern here is the attention created by a crowd at the gates.
The phrase indicates service or assignments apportioned by the day; “by daily turns” is an alternative.
ξενία can denote hospitality or guest accommodation; the practical task here is arranging places to stay.

passages.text: When Peter had said this, they were compelled to consent, saying, “It does not greatly distress us, lord, to do this, because we are commanded by you. First, being worthy, you were chosen by God’s providence to understand everything well and to give sound counsel. Besides, the necessity of going ahead separates us from you for at most two days. Even these are a long time when it comes to not seeing you, Peter our lord. Yet we reflect that those sent much farther ahead will be more distressed, since they have been commanded to wait longer for you in each city, grieving because they are deprived for a longer time of seeing your much-longed-for face. Although we are no less disheartened than they, we do not object to doing as you command, because it is beneficial.” Nevertheless, after saying this, they went ahead, having instructions to speak at the first inn to the crowd traveling with them, so that, once separated from one another, they might enter the cities in scattered groups.

lexical_decisions.rationale: συντίθεμαι here means agreeing to a proposal; the passive of ἀναγκάζω conveys their reluctant necessity.
In this context ἐπὶ τὸ πολύ is taken as marking an upper limit. “As a rule, for two days” is also grammatically possible.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πάντα καλῶς νοεῖν τε καὶ συμβουλεύειν
lexical_decisions.chosen: to understand everything well and to give sound counsel
lexical_decisions.rationale: πάντα is taken with the coordinated infinitives, while συμβουλεύειν denotes advising rather than merely deliberating privately.
προπέμπω here refers to dispatching people in advance, and πολὺ μακράν emphasizes the greater distance.
περιπόθητος expresses intense longing or dearness, and πρόσωπον retains the concrete image of the face.

lexical_decisions.chosen: once separated from one another ... in scattered groups
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adverb depicts dispersion rather than an organized mass entry; “having become scattered from one another” is the more literal wording.

passages.text: After they had gone, I, Clement, was exceedingly glad that he had told me to remain with him. I responded, “I thank God that you did not send me away as you did my companions, since I would have cried out in pain.” But he said, “What, then? If a need should arise for you to be sent somewhere for the sake of instruction, will you die just because, for your benefit, you are separated from me for a short time? Would you not instead, after talking it over with yourself, cheerfully undertake to bear what has been commanded of you because necessity required it? Or do you not know that friends are always together in their memories, even if they are separated in body, while some who are together in body are, because of forgetfulness, far away in soul from their friends?”

lexical_decisions.chosen: I would have cried out in pain
lexical_decisions.rationale: The pluperfect with ἄν presents the unreal result, while the participle supplies the pain or anguish accompanying the outcry.
μαθήματα can concern lessons, learning, or teaching; the Greek does not specify whether Clement would primarily receive or provide the instruction.
The adverb indicates that the temporary separation serves an advantageous or expedient purpose.

lexical_decisions.chosen: after talking it over with yourself
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase literally describes conversing with oneself and contextually implies inward reasoning or self-exhortation.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: σύνεισιν αἰεὶ οἱ φίλοι ταῖς μνήμαις
lexical_decisions.chosen: friends are always together in their memories
lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative presents memory as the sphere or means by which absent friends remain together.

lexical_decisions.chosen: are ... far away in soul from their friends
lexical_decisions.rationale: The accusative marks respect—“as to their souls”—while ἀποδημέω supplies the image of being away from home.

source_issues.issue: The selected edition prints a raised point between πορευθέντων and οὖν, interrupting the genitive-absolute construction. The translation treats the words as one continuous construction while preserving the printed wording; no alteration of the Greek letters is proposed.

passages.text: And I answered, “Do not suppose, then, my lord, that my distress would have been irrational; rather, it would have rested on entirely sound reasoning. For since I have you, my lord, in place of everyone—father, mother, brothers, and relatives—you who, for God’s sake, became for me the cause of the truth that saves, I receive the greatest consolation by having you in place of everyone. Moreover, because I fear the desire natural to my youthful prime, I was anxious that, if separated from you, young man that I am, I might prove weaker than desire. Yet now I have such resistance in this matter that, even if I were to leave you because of some wrath from God, it would be impossible for me to prove weaker than desire. But since it is far better and safer for me to be with you, the one whom my mind has rightly determined beforehand to revere, I therefore pray to be with you always. Furthermore, I remember you saying in Caesarea, ‘If anyone wishes to accompany me, let him accompany me reverently.’ By ‘reverently,’ you said you meant causing no one grief in matters relating to God—for example, by leaving behind parents, a like-minded wife, or any companions devoted to reverence for God. Thus I am in every respect a suitable traveling companion for you. Even if you grant me the greatest favors, you still permit me to perform the duties of servants.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: my distress would have been irrational
lexical_decisions.rationale: Literally, Clement speaks of “suffering the things of sorrow”; the rendering expresses the same claim in natural English without reducing λύπη to physical pain.
διά with the accusative is causal here. “Because of God” is more literal; “through God” would normally require the genitive.
The participle directly characterizes the truth as saving and should not be reduced to merely helpful or correct teaching.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῆς ἀκμῆς τὴν ἐκ φύσεως ἐπιθυμίαν
lexical_decisions.chosen: the desire natural to my youthful prime
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀκμή denotes one’s prime or youthful vigor, while ἐκ φύσεως presents the desire as natural to that stage of life.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁ νοῦς μου αἰδεῖσθαι εὐλόγως προείληφεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: whom my mind has rightly determined beforehand to revere
lexical_decisions.rationale: προλαμβάνω here indicates a prior resolve or settled choice, and αἰδεῖσθαι conveys reverence or respectful regard.

lexical_decisions.chosen: causing no one grief in matters relating to God
lexical_decisions.rationale: κατὰ θεόν can mean “in relation to God,” “according to God,” or “in a godly matter.” The following examples concern obligations to people sharing or connected with devotion to God.
ὁμόφρων describes one who shares the same outlook or purpose, here likely including religious commitment.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰς δούλων μοι ὑπηρεσίας συγχωρεῖς ποιεῖν
lexical_decisions.chosen: you ... permit me to perform the duties of servants
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase denotes subordinate personal service. “Slaves’ services” would make the bonded-status nuance more explicit, but “servants” follows the supplied wording policy.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Even if you grant me the greatest favors
lexical_decisions.rationale: εἰ καί is read concessively. It may alternatively imply that permission to serve is itself among the greatest favors, but that relationship is not syntactically explicit.

source_issues.source_quote: ὅπερ νῦν οὕτως ἐνστάσεως ἔχω, κἂν κατὰ τινὰ χόλον θεοῦ ἀποστῆναί σου ἀδύνατον εἰ ἥττων ἐπιθυμίας ἔσομαι
source_issues.issue: The syntax is compressed, particularly the attachment of ὅπερ, ἀδύνατον, and the final εἰ-clause. The translation takes οὕτως ... ἀδύνατον as a result construction and the εἰ-clause as expressing what would be impossible: becoming weaker than desire. Alternatively, ἀδύνατον may qualify ἀποστῆναί σου (“it is impossible to leave you”), with the final εἰ-clause resuming Clement’s earlier anxiety. No conjectural alteration has been adopted.

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Contested terms

The following terms appear frequently and carry heavy theological
weight. Our default rendering and rationale are recorded here.
Per-verse variance is documented in the individual YAML files.

| Χριστός *Christos* | Messiah where independently titular; Christ in the name forms "Jesus Christ" / "Christ Jesus" | Christ, Messiah | Preserves the title's Hebraic messianic meaning while using the recognizable conventional English personal name |
| κύριος *Kyrios* | Lord | LORD, Master | Matches covenantal and NT usage |
| δοῦλος *doulos* | servant | bondservant, slave | Uses reader-facing "servant" consistently; documents bonded-status and ownership nuance in notes/audit metadata |

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.
